newsitem.title: UK: UK stocks outlook - FTSE 100 to take lead from Dow.
newsitem.headline: UK stocks outlook - FTSE 100 to take lead from Dow.

text.p: The UK stock market looks poised to reach fresh high ground next week, with growing optimism over the U.S. economy fuelling stock market records in New York and dragging UK shares to unprecedented peaks.

"Everyone is transfixed with Wall Street going ballisticand that will continue to be the driving factor" said Bob Semple, strategist at NatWest Securities. "It's hard to see what will trip the market up."

The Dow has set five consecutive record closes and U.S. blue-chips were roaring higher again on Friday, after producer price data came in weaker than expected. Recent economic data has lent support to the view that U.S. interest rates may be held unchanged after the next FOMC meeting on July 2.

The FTSE 100 index has set its own succession of record highs, encouraged by U.S. stock market strength. Leading British shares were up nearly three percent on the week and up 24.9 points to 4,782.3 on the day by 1430 GMT on Friday.
"The market looks like it is getting carried away in the short term but if the U.S. carries on up then we're bound to be dragged up with it," Semple said.
Supporting factors will continue to be the historically high levels of liquidity in the market and fervent bid activity.
"New highs are almost certainly in the offing," said Jeremy Batstone, head of research at NatWest Stockbrokers. "The only concern is a possible pause in the trend after a strong run."

The flotation of British mutual insurer Norwich Union NRU.CN NU.L will kick-start the week on Monday with a likely value of around 5.5 billion stg. Norwich Union will become Britain's third-largest quoted insurer behind Prudential Corp and Royal & Sun Alliance and is almost a certainty to enter the FTSE 100 index.

Financial bookmakers, City Index are taking bets on a first day closing price of between 346-354p for Norwich Union shares with the company expecting the public offer price to be between 240-290 pence.
Elsewhere, analysts will be keeping one eye on the EU leaders summit in Amsterdam on June 16-17 and an attempt to reach a consensus on monetary union and the budget stability pact.
"It looks as though the stability pact will be signed but we may see some volatility in the currency markets," said Batstone.
In the midst of recent euro-jitters, UK financial markets have benefited from their safe-haven status and analysts think it unlikely sterling will retreat far from its lofty heights.

The performance of sterling, which is trading around a five-year high against major European currencies will also set the stage for British Steel's annual results on Monday, one of the companies hardest hit by the impact of the currency on exports.

Profits are expected to be slashed from 1.1 billion stg to around 460 million stg and the company may also announce severe job cuts. The shares have fallen around 20 percent in the last 10 months amid a series of earnings estimates downgrades.
In a quiet week for corporate results, Thames Water on Tuesday is the only other FTSE company reporting next week.
Across the Atlantic, Group of Seven financial leaders will meet at the weekend in Denver to focus on market redorms and regulation.
"People will be wanting to know what they think about Japan's trade surplus building up against the U.S," Batstone said. "And especially the relationship between the yen and the dollar."
U.S. CPI numbers on Monday will be the most closely watched indicators on hopes that the data will add to the growing optimism over the U.S. rate outlook.
Barring any upset from the U.S., UK shares continue to be supported by a firm bond market which has remained stable in the face of increased euro uncertainty.
Domestic economic data will include UK retail sales data for May which will provide the first indications as to how account holders of Alliance and Leicester spent their recent windfalls.
"It will have implications for the budget and interest rates," Semple said.
Caution over the government's first budget on July 2 could begin to affect investment decisions, traders said.

"There is still a lot of uncertainty over the budget," Batstone said. "The pressure is on the Chancellor (of the Exchequer) to reign in consumer spending and if the Chancellor gets tough, then it may forstall any further interest rate rises."
"At the moment people seem to be remarkably calm about the budget," agreed Semple. "But people will be getting more nervous as the date draws near."
